meta_desc: Solve Grade 3 subtraction word problems: spot the three story types, borrow across 3 digits, check by adding back, then try a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Most Grade 3 children can subtract on paper but freeze the moment the sum hides inside a story. Here are the three subtraction story types, how to spot each one, and a quick quiz to test your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 3 child a bare sum like 452 − 178 and, with a bit of borrowing practice, they will get there. Wrap that same sum inside a story — ‘Riya had ₹452 and spent ₹178 on a story book, how much is left?’ — and half the class stalls. They are not stuck on the subtraction. They are stuck on knowing that it is subtraction. That gap is exactly what Grade 3 subtraction word problems are meant to close, and it is a different skill from computing the answer.

The good news: nearly every subtraction story in Grade 3 is one of just three types. Once a child can name the type, the number sentence almost writes itself. Numbers at this level usually stay under 1,000, so a firm grip on 3-digit subtraction with borrowing is all the calculation you need.

The three subtraction story types

I teach these by the question they secretly ask, not by keywords. Keyword-hunting (‘left means minus’) breaks the moment a problem says ‘how many more’ and the child adds. Meaning is safer than tricks.

1. Take-away — something is removed

The classic. You start with an amount, some of it goes, and you want what remains. ‘A shopkeeper had 340 eggs and sold 165. How many are left?’ Start − part that left = what remains. Here 340 − 165 = 175 eggs.

2. Compare — how many more or fewer

Nothing is removed here; two amounts sit side by side and you want the difference. ‘Aarav has 210 stamps and Meera has 145. How many more does Aarav have?’ The word ‘more’ tempts children to add, but you are finding a gap, so it is 210 − 145 = 65 stamps. This is the type most children get wrong, and it is worth extra practice.

3. Missing-part — had some, have this, how many gone

You know the start and the end, and the middle is missing. ‘A water tank held 500 litres. Now 320 litres are left. How much was used?’ Start − end = the missing part, so 500 − 320 = 180 litres. Same subtraction, but the story hands you the answer and hides the action.

How to read a subtraction word problem

Before any borrowing happens, I ask children to do three small things. They take under a minute and they prevent almost every ‘I added instead’ mistake.

  • Find the two numbers and underline them. In ‘452 and 178’ those are your start and your part.
  • Decide which is bigger. In subtraction the bigger number goes on top, always. This alone stops the common 178 − 452 muddle.
  • Name the story type out loud — take-away, compare, or missing-part — and only then write the sentence.

Borrowing inside the story

Once the sentence is written, it is ordinary 3-digit subtraction. Take ₹452 − ₹178. The ones column asks 2 − 8, which we cannot do, so we borrow one ten: the 2 becomes 12 and the tens 5 becomes 4. Now 12 − 8 = 4. In the tens, 4 − 7 again needs a borrow from the hundreds: 14 − 7 = 7, and the hundreds 4 became 3, giving 3 − 1 = 2. Answer: ₹274 left.

Borrowing across two columns trips up a lot of Grade 3 children, especially when there is a zero in the middle, as in 500 − 320. Teach the zero case slowly and with real objects or a place-value chart before rushing to the algorithm. In my experience, the child who understands why the 5 shrinks to a 4 makes far fewer silly slips than the one who just memorised ‘cross out and add ten’.

Always check by adding back

This is the habit I care about most, and it is the one most often skipped. Subtraction and addition undo each other, so the answer plus the number you took away should return the number you started with. If 452 − 178 = 274, then 274 + 178 should equal 452 — and it does. If it does not, there is a borrowing slip to hunt down.

Adding back turns a child from someone who hopes they are right into someone who knows. It costs ten seconds and catches the majority of errors. Make it non-negotiable, the way a cricketer checks their grip before every ball.

A quick worked example, start to finish

‘A library had 615 books. It lent out 248 during the week. How many remain?’ Story type: take-away. Sentence: 615 − 248. Borrowing gives 615 − 248 = 367. Check: 367 + 248 = 615. It matches, so 367 books remain. Notice how naming the type came first and the arithmetic came last — that order is the whole game.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight questions below cover all three story types, with numbers up to 1,000 and a few that need double borrowing. Let your child solve each one, then read the explanation together for any they miss — pay special attention to the ‘how many more’ compare questions. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded subtraction word problems with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Subtraction Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight story problems covering take-away, compare and missing-part subtraction with numbers to 1,000. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A shopkeeper had 340 eggs and sold 165. How many eggs are left?
questions.explanation: This is take-away: 340 − 165. Borrow in the ones and tens to get 175 eggs.

questions.q: Aarav has 210 stamps and Meera has 145. How many more stamps does Aarav have?
questions.explanation: This is a compare problem, so find the gap: 210 − 145 = 65. The word 'more' does not mean add here.

questions.q: A tank held 500 litres. Now 320 litres are left. How many litres were used?
In 452 − 178, why do we borrow in the ones column?
questions.explanation: The ones ask 2 − 8, which we cannot do, so we borrow one ten to make it 12 − 8.

questions.q: A library had 615 books and lent out 248. How many remain?
You solved 452 − 178 = 274. Which sum checks the answer?
questions.explanation: Add the answer to the number taken away: 274 + 178 should equal 452, the number you started with.

questions.q: Riya had ₹760 and spent ₹385. How much money is left?
questions.explanation: Take-away: 760 − 385 = 375 rupees, using borrowing in the ones and tens.

questions.q: A train has 428 seats and 236 are booked. How many seats are still empty?

faq.q: How do I know when a word problem needs subtraction?
faq.a: Look at what the story is asking, not single keywords. If something is removed, if you need the difference between two amounts, or if a part is missing between a start and an end, it is subtraction. Naming the story type — take-away, compare or missing-part — is more reliable than hunting for the word 'left'.

faq.q: Why does my child add when the question says 'how many more'?
faq.a: Because 'more' feels like addition. But 'how many more' asks for the gap between two amounts, which is a compare problem and needs subtraction. Practise a few of these on their own until the child pauses at 'more' instead of reaching straight for the plus sign.

faq.q: What size numbers should Grade 3 subtraction word problems use?
faq.a: Mostly up to 1,000, which means 3-digit subtraction with borrowing. Zeros in the middle, like 500 − 320, deserve extra practice because double borrowing across a zero is where most slips happen.

faq.q: How should my child check a subtraction answer?
faq.a: Add back. The answer plus the number that was taken away should return the starting number: if 452 − 178 = 274, then 274 + 178 must equal 452. If it does not match, there is a borrowing mistake to find. Make this a fixed habit.
